intro.title: Keys and relationships
intro.bodyMarkdown:
Real databases split their data over several tables. This quest's shop has five: `customers`, `orders`, `order_items`, `products` and `employees`. Open **Tables** to see how they fit together.

Why not one big table? An order would then repeat the customer's name and city on every line, and a customer who moved would need changing in many places. Splitting the data stores each fact **once**, and the tables point to each other instead.

Every table has an `id` column, its **primary key**: a number that identifies one row and is never repeated. Other tables refer to a row by that number. In `orders`, `customer_id` holds the `id` of the customer who placed the order. A column like that is a **foreign key**.

```
SELECT id, customer_id, employee_id, order_date FROM orders;
```

So order 1 has `customer_id` 1: it was placed by the customer whose `id` is 1, Ana Silva. In the same way, `employee_id` points to `employees`, `order_items` points to both `orders` and `products`, and `employees.manager_id` points to another employee.

Without joins, following a key takes two steps: look up the id, then use it.

```
SELECT id FROM customers WHERE name = 'Ana Silva';
SELECT id, order_date FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 1;
```

The next stage does both steps in one query. In this one, practise reading the keys.

intro.title: INNER JOIN
intro.bodyMarkdown:
`JOIN` combines rows from two tables in one query. `ON` says which rows belong together, usually a foreign key equal to a primary key:

```
SELECT orders.id, orders.order_date, customers.name
FROM orders
JOIN customers ON orders.customer_id = customers.id;
```

For each order, SQLite finds the customer whose `id` equals the order's `customer_id`, and puts the two rows side by side. The result has one row per matching pair.

Because both tables have columns called `id` and `name`, write `table.column` to say which one you mean: `orders.id`, `customers.name`. It is a good habit even when the name is unique.

`JOIN` on its own means `INNER JOIN`: only rows that **have** a match appear. Customers who never ordered aren't in the result above, because no order points to them. (The `LEFT JOIN` stage keeps them.)

Getting `ON` wrong is a common join mistake. `ON orders.id = customers.id` runs without an error, but pairs order 1 with customer 1, order 2 with customer 2, and so on, which means nothing. Always join a foreign key to the key it points to.

Which table comes first doesn't change an inner join's rows: `FROM customers JOIN orders ON …` gives the same pairs.

intro.title: Table aliases
intro.bodyMarkdown:
Writing `orders.` and `customers.` before every column gets long. A **table alias** gives a table a short name for the rest of the query:

```
SELECT o.id, o.order_date, c.name
FROM orders AS o
JOIN customers AS c ON o.customer_id = c.id;
```

The `AS` is optional for tables, so `FROM orders o JOIN customers c` means the same. Short aliases like `o`, `c` and `p` are the usual style, and you will see them in most real queries.

Once a table has an alias, use the alias everywhere in that query. `FROM orders o … WHERE orders.status = 'shipped'` gives the error **no such column: orders.status**, because inside this query the table is now called `o`.

If a column name exists in both tables and you leave out the table, SQLite can't guess which one you mean:

```
-- This gives an error: ambiguous column name: id
SELECT id, name
FROM orders o
JOIN customers c ON o.customer_id = c.id;
```

The fix is to say which table: `o.id` or `c.id`. Columns that exist in only one table work without a prefix, but adding it keeps a query readable when it grows.

When you show two columns with the same name, give them different names with `AS`, so the result is clear: `SELECT o.id AS order_id, c.id AS customer_id`.

intro.title: Filtering and sorting joins
intro.bodyMarkdown:
A join gives you rows with the columns of both tables, and everything you know still works on them. `WHERE` can test a column from either table, and `ORDER BY` can sort by any of them.

Ana's orders, found by her name instead of her id:

```
SELECT o.id, o.order_date
FROM orders o
JOIN customers c ON o.customer_id = c.id
WHERE c.name = 'Ana Silva';
```

This is the two-step lookup from the first stage, done in one query. The order is always the same: `FROM` and `JOIN`, then `WHERE`, then `ORDER BY` and `LIMIT`.

Shipped orders, sorted by customer and then by date:

```
SELECT c.name, o.order_date
FROM orders o
JOIN customers c ON o.customer_id = c.id
WHERE o.status = 'shipped'
ORDER BY c.name, o.order_date;
```

You can also calculate with columns from both tables, and sort by the result. Here are the order lines worth more than 20, biggest first:

```
SELECT i.order_id, p.name, ROUND(i.quantity * p.price, 2) AS line_total
FROM order_items i
JOIN products p ON i.product_id = p.id
WHERE i.quantity * p.price > 20
ORDER BY line_total DESC, i.order_id;
```

intro.title: Totals across tables
intro.bodyMarkdown:
Joins and `GROUP BY` work well together: join first to bring in the names, then group and count.

```
SELECT c.name, COUNT(*) AS orders
FROM orders o
JOIN customers c ON o.customer_id = c.id
GROUP BY c.id, c.name;
```

Why group by `c.id` as well as `c.name`? Two customers could share a name, and grouping by the name alone would add their orders together. Grouping by the id keeps each customer separate, and adding the name lets you show it.

Totals often need a calculation from both tables. The total of each order is the sum of quantity times price over its lines:

```
SELECT i.order_id, ROUND(SUM(i.quantity * p.price), 2) AS total
FROM order_items i
JOIN products p ON i.product_id = p.id
GROUP BY i.order_id;
```

`WHERE`, `HAVING` and `ORDER BY` work as before. The rows are joined, then filtered by `WHERE`, then grouped, then the groups are filtered by `HAVING`.

One thing to notice: a customer with no orders doesn't appear at all, not even with 0. The inner join dropped them before the counting began. The `LEFT JOIN` stage fixes that.

intro.title: LEFT JOIN
intro.bodyMarkdown:
An inner join drops rows with no match: Finn and Grace never ordered, so they vanish from every query so far. `LEFT JOIN` keeps **every row of the left table** (the one in `FROM`), matched or not:

```
SELECT c.name, o.id AS order_id
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id;
```

Customers with orders get one row per order, as before. Finn and Grace get one row each, with `NULL` in every column from `orders`, because there was nothing to fill them with.

This makes counting with zeros possible. Count a column from the right table, not the rows: `COUNT(*)` would count Finn's single row and say 1, but `COUNT(o.id)` skips the `NULL` and says 0.

```
SELECT c.name, COUNT(o.id) AS orders
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
GROUP BY c.id, c.name;
```

`SUM` over no rows gives `NULL`, not 0, so wrap it: `COALESCE(SUM(i.quantity), 0)`.

Where you put a condition matters. To count only shipped orders but keep every customer, put the condition in `ON`: `LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id AND o.status = 'shipped'`. In `WHERE`, the test `o.status = 'shipped'` is not true for the `NULL` rows (it is unknown), so they are thrown away and the query acts like an inner join again.

Which table goes first matters too: the one in `FROM` is the one that is kept whole. SQLite 3.39 and later also has `RIGHT JOIN`, which keeps the right table instead, but you can always swap the tables and use `LEFT JOIN`, which is what most people do.

intro.title: Rows with no match
intro.bodyMarkdown:
Some of the most useful questions are about what is missing: customers who never ordered, products nobody bought, staff with no sales. A `LEFT JOIN` finds them, because the unmatched rows are the ones with `NULL` on the right side.

```
SELECT c.name
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
WHERE o.id IS NULL;
```

Read it as: take every customer, attach their orders if they have any, then keep only the rows where no order was attached. Test a column that can't be `NULL` in a real match, like the right table's `id`.

This `WHERE` is fine, unlike the one in the last stage. There, `WHERE o.status = 'shipped'` threw the unmatched rows away by accident. Here, `WHERE o.id IS NULL` keeps only the unmatched rows, on purpose.

You can combine both ideas. Customers with no **shipped** order: put the status in `ON`, so only shipped orders can match, then keep the rows that found none:

```
SELECT c.name
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id AND o.status = 'shipped'
WHERE o.id IS NULL;
```

Remember to use `IS NULL`, never `= NULL`, which is never true.

intro.title: Three or more tables
intro.bodyMarkdown:
A query can join as many tables as it needs. Each `JOIN` adds one more table to the rows built so far, with its own `ON`:

```
SELECT o.id, c.name AS customer, e.name AS employee
FROM orders o
JOIN customers c ON o.customer_id = c.id
JOIN employees e ON o.employee_id = e.id;
```

Follow the keys like a path. To get from a customer to the products they bought, go customers → orders → order_items → products, one join per step:

```
SELECT c.name AS customer, p.name AS product, i.quantity
FROM customers c
JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
JOIN order_items i ON i.order_id = o.id
JOIN products p ON i.product_id = p.id;
```

Everything else works the same: filter with `WHERE`, group, total and sort. How much each customer spent:

```
SELECT c.name, ROUND(SUM(i.quantity * p.price), 2) AS spent
FROM customers c
JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
JOIN order_items i ON i.order_id = o.id
JOIN products p ON i.product_id = p.id
GROUP BY c.id, c.name
ORDER BY spent DESC;
```

To keep customers who never ordered, make the first join a `LEFT JOIN`, and the joins after it too. A plain `JOIN` later in the chain would need a match for the `NULL` rows, find none, and drop them again.

Long joins are easier to get right step by step: run the first join, look at the rows, then add the next.

intro.title: Joining a table to itself
intro.bodyMarkdown:
In `employees`, `manager_id` holds the `id` of another employee. To show each employee next to their manager's name, join the table to **itself**, with two different aliases:

```
SELECT e.name AS employee, m.name AS manager
FROM employees e
JOIN employees m ON e.manager_id = m.id;
```

Think of `e` and `m` as two copies of the same table: `e` plays the employee, `m` plays the manager. The aliases are required here, because both copies have the same name.

Maria Lopez has no manager, so the inner join drops her. Use `LEFT JOIN` to keep her, with `NULL` (or a `COALESCE` text) as her manager.

Grouping by the manager copy counts the size of each team:

```
SELECT m.name AS manager, COUNT(*) AS reports
FROM employees e
JOIN employees m ON e.manager_id = m.id
GROUP BY m.id, m.name;
```

Self-joins aren't only for managers. Any time you want to pair rows of a table with other rows of the same table, such as products in the same category, join it to itself. Add `a.id < b.id` to the `ON` so each pair appears once, and a row isn't paired with itself.

```
SELECT a.name AS product_1, b.name AS product_2
FROM products a
JOIN products b ON a.category = b.category AND a.id < b.id;
```

intro.title: Many-to-many
intro.bodyMarkdown:
A customer has many orders, but each order has one customer: that is **one-to-many**, and a foreign key in `orders` is enough.

Orders and products are different. An order can contain many products, and a product can appear in many orders. That is **many-to-many**, and no single column can hold it. Instead, a third table sits in the middle: `order_items`, with one row per pair, plus facts about the pair, like the quantity. A table like this is called a **junction table**.

To go from orders to products, you always pass through the junction table:

```
SELECT o.id, p.name, i.quantity
FROM orders o
JOIN order_items i ON i.order_id = o.id
JOIN products p ON i.product_id = p.id;
```

Because a product can be in many orders, and a customer can buy it more than once, counts through a junction table often need `COUNT(DISTINCT …)`. How many different customers bought each product:

```
SELECT p.name, COUNT(DISTINCT o.customer_id) AS customers
FROM products p
JOIN order_items i ON i.product_id = p.id
JOIN orders o ON i.order_id = o.id
GROUP BY p.id, p.name;
```

A self-join of the junction table answers "what is bought together?": two lines of the same order, with different products.

```
SELECT i1.order_id, i1.product_id AS product_1, i2.product_id AS product_2
FROM order_items i1
JOIN order_items i2 ON i1.order_id = i2.order_id AND i1.product_id < i2.product_id;
```

intro.bodyMarkdown:
The marketing team wants to understand the customers: who orders, who spends, who has gone quiet, and what each category attracts.

Remember: customers who never ordered only appear with a `LEFT JOIN`, and their totals need `COALESCE`.
intro.sandboxCode:

challenges.title: Easy: Order counts
challenges.promptMarkdown: Show every customer's `name` and number of orders (`orders`), including 0. Most first, then by name.
challenges.hint: `LEFT JOIN orders`, `COUNT(o.id)`, `ORDER BY orders DESC, c.name`.
challenges.solution:
SELECT c.name, COUNT(o.id) AS orders
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
GROUP BY c.id, c.name
ORDER BY orders DESC, c.name;

challenges.title: Medium: Gone quiet
challenges.promptMarkdown: The team wants to email customers who never ordered. Show their `name`, `city` and `joined` date, earliest joined first.
challenges.hint: `LEFT JOIN orders … WHERE o.id IS NULL ORDER BY c.joined`.
challenges.solution:
SELECT c.name, c.city, c.joined
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
WHERE o.id IS NULL
ORDER BY c.joined;

challenges.title: Medium: Average order
challenges.promptMarkdown: For each customer who ordered, show their `name`, number of orders (`orders`) and average order value (`average_order`: total spent divided by orders, 2 decimals). Highest average first.
challenges.hint: Join all four tables; `COUNT(DISTINCT o.id)` counts orders, not lines. `ROUND(SUM(i.quantity * p.price) / COUNT(DISTINCT o.id), 2)`.
challenges.solution:
SELECT c.name, COUNT(DISTINCT o.id) AS orders,
       ROUND(SUM(i.quantity * p.price) / COUNT(DISTINCT o.id), 2) AS average_order
FROM customers c
JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
JOIN order_items i ON i.order_id = o.id
JOIN products p ON i.product_id = p.id
GROUP BY c.id, c.name
ORDER BY average_order DESC;

challenges.title: Medium: Category reach
challenges.promptMarkdown: For each category that was ordered, show the `category`, how many different customers bought from it (`customers`) and the items sold (`items`). Most customers first, then by category.
challenges.hint: `COUNT(DISTINCT o.customer_id)`, `SUM(i.quantity)`, `GROUP BY p.category`.
challenges.solution:
SELECT p.category, COUNT(DISTINCT o.customer_id) AS customers, SUM(i.quantity) AS items
FROM products p
JOIN order_items i ON i.product_id = p.id
JOIN orders o ON i.order_id = o.id
GROUP BY p.category
ORDER BY customers DESC, p.category;

challenges.title: Hard: Shipped and not
challenges.promptMarkdown: Show every customer's `name` with their number of shipped orders (`shipped`) and other orders (`not_shipped`), including customers with none (0 and 0). In name order.
challenges.hint: LEFT JOIN orders, then `SUM(CASE WHEN o.status = 'shipped' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)` and `SUM(CASE WHEN o.status <> 'shipped' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)`.
challenges.solution:
SELECT c.name,
  SUM(CASE WHEN o.status = 'shipped' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS shipped,
  SUM(CASE WHEN o.status <> 'shipped' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS not_shipped
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
GROUP BY c.id, c.name
ORDER BY c.name;

challenges.title: Hard: Best customers
challenges.promptMarkdown: Show the customers who spent more than 100 on shipped orders: `name` and `spent` (2 decimals). Highest first.
challenges.hint: Join all four tables, `WHERE o.status = 'shipped'`, then `HAVING SUM(i.quantity * p.price) > 100`.
challenges.solution:
SELECT c.name, ROUND(SUM(i.quantity * p.price), 2) AS spent
FROM customers c
JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
JOIN order_items i ON i.order_id = o.id
JOIN products p ON i.product_id = p.id
WHERE o.status = 'shipped'
GROUP BY c.id, c.name
HAVING SUM(i.quantity * p.price) > 100
ORDER BY spent DESC;

intro.title: Hard side quest: Sales team review
intro.bodyMarkdown:
It's review time for the staff. Maria, the manager, wants to see who works for whom, how much each person and each team sold, and how much is still waiting to ship.

These queries join `employees` to itself and to the order tables. Build them step by step in the sandbox.

challenges.title: Easy: Staff list
challenges.promptMarkdown: Show every employee's `name`, `role` and their manager's name as `manager` (`(none)` for the top boss), in employee id order.
challenges.hint: `LEFT JOIN employees m ON e.manager_id = m.id`, `COALESCE(m.name, '(none)')`, `ORDER BY e.id`.
challenges.solution:
SELECT e.name, e.role, COALESCE(m.name, '(none)') AS manager
FROM employees e
LEFT JOIN employees m ON e.manager_id = m.id
ORDER BY e.id;

challenges.title: Medium: Everyone's numbers
challenges.promptMarkdown: Show every employee's `name`, the orders they handled (`orders`) and the value of those orders (`sales`, 2 decimals), with 0 for both if they handled none. Highest sales first, then by name.
challenges.hint: LEFT JOIN all the way: orders, order_items, products. `COUNT(DISTINCT o.id)` and `ROUND(COALESCE(SUM(i.quantity * p.price), 0), 2)`.
challenges.solution:
SELECT e.name, COUNT(DISTINCT o.id) AS orders,
       ROUND(COALESCE(SUM(i.quantity * p.price), 0), 2) AS sales
FROM employees e
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.employee_id = e.id
LEFT JOIN order_items i ON i.order_id = o.id
LEFT JOIN products p ON i.product_id = p.id
GROUP BY e.id, e.name
ORDER BY sales DESC, e.name;

challenges.title: Medium: Shipped by sales staff
challenges.promptMarkdown: For employees with the role `Sales`, show each `name` and the value of their shipped orders (`shipped_sales`, 2 decimals). Only those with shipped orders, highest first.
challenges.hint: `WHERE e.role = 'Sales' AND o.status = 'shipped'`, then group by employee.
challenges.solution:
SELECT e.name, ROUND(SUM(i.quantity * p.price), 2) AS shipped_sales
FROM employees e
JOIN orders o ON o.employee_id = e.id
JOIN order_items i ON i.order_id = o.id
JOIN products p ON i.product_id = p.id
WHERE e.role = 'Sales' AND o.status = 'shipped'
GROUP BY e.id, e.name
ORDER BY shipped_sales DESC;

challenges.title: Hard: Team totals
challenges.promptMarkdown: For each manager, show their name as `manager` and the value of the orders handled by the people who report directly to them (`team_sales`, 2 decimals). Highest first.
challenges.hint: employees e JOIN employees m (the manager), then orders on `o.employee_id = e.id`, order_items and products. Group by the manager.
challenges.solution:
SELECT m.name AS manager, ROUND(SUM(i.quantity * p.price), 2) AS team_sales
FROM employees e
JOIN employees m ON e.manager_id = m.id
JOIN orders o ON o.employee_id = e.id
JOIN order_items i ON i.order_id = o.id
JOIN products p ON i.product_id = p.id
GROUP BY m.id, m.name
ORDER BY team_sales DESC;

challenges.title: Hard: Shipped or waiting
challenges.promptMarkdown: For each employee who handled orders, show `name`, the value of their shipped orders (`shipped`) and of their other orders (`not_shipped`), both 2 decimals. In name order.
challenges.hint: `ROUND(SUM(CASE WHEN o.status = 'shipped' THEN i.quantity * p.price ELSE 0 END), 2)` and the same with `<>`.
challenges.solution:
SELECT e.name,
  ROUND(SUM(CASE WHEN o.status = 'shipped' THEN i.quantity * p.price ELSE 0 END), 2) AS shipped,
  ROUND(SUM(CASE WHEN o.status <> 'shipped' THEN i.quantity * p.price ELSE 0 END), 2) AS not_shipped
FROM employees e
JOIN orders o ON o.employee_id = e.id
JOIN order_items i ON i.order_id = o.id
JOIN products p ON i.product_id = p.id
GROUP BY e.id, e.name
ORDER BY e.name;

challenges.title: Hard: Shared customers
challenges.promptMarkdown: Show each customer who was served by two or more different employees: `name` and the number of employees (`employees`). Most first, then by name.
challenges.hint: `COUNT(DISTINCT o.employee_id)`, `HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT o.employee_id) >= 2`.

SELECT c.name, COUNT(DISTINCT o.employee_id) AS employees
FROM customers c
JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
GROUP BY c.id, c.name
HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT o.employee_id) >= 2
ORDER BY employees DESC, c.name;
